mentions.quote: so said Manu
mentions.role: lawgiver cited as authority for the rule on bride-substitution

mentions.quote: Manu has declared to be not punishable
mentions.role: lawgiver cited as authority for the rule exempting certain cattle from fines

mentions.quote: Manu has declared this not to be theft
mentions.role: lawgiver cited as authority for the rule permitting taking fruit, roots, and grass

mentions.quote: Manu has not declared a punishment
mentions.role: lawgiver cited as authority for exempting certain vehicle accidents from punishment

entities.description: The primordial lawgiver whose pronouncements are invoked throughout the chapter as the supreme authority for legal and dharmic rulings.
entities.justification: Manu is named four times in the window as the originating authority behind specific legal decisions, confirming his role as the foundational figure of the text.

mentions.quote: the master, like Yama, having himself abandoned what is dear and not dear, should act with the conduct of Yama
mentions.role: divine exemplar invoked as a model of impartial judgment for a king

entities.description: The god of death and cosmic judge whose impartiality and self-control are held up as the ideal standard for a king administering justice.
entities.justification: Yama is named twice within a single verse as the explicit divine model the king must emulate, grounding him as a normative exemplar.

mentions.quote: A king who desires the station of Indra and fame that is imperishable and unchanging must not overlook for even a moment a violent criminal
mentions.role: cosmic reward representing the highest royal aspiration for a just king

mentions.quote: he is a partaker of the world of Indra
mentions.role: heavenly realm promised to a king who successfully suppresses crime in his domain

entities.description: King of the gods whose station and realm are held out as the supreme reward for a king who diligently enforces the law and suppresses criminals.
entities.justification: Indra appears in two distinct verses as the eschatological reward for righteous kingship, making him a key motivational figure in this legal context.

mentions.quote: he was created by the Self-existent One for the service of a Brahmana
mentions.role: cosmic creator whose primordial act of creation grounds the cosmic-dharmic justification of Shudra servitude

entities.description: The self-existent creator deity (Brahman / Svayambhu) invoked to provide cosmological sanction for the varna hierarchy and the Shudra's duty of service.
entities.justification: The Self-existent One is cited as the ultimate author of the social order prescribing Shudra servitude, grounding an ontological claim with divine authority.

mentions.quote: A Kshatriya who insults a Brahmana deserves a fine of one hundred
mentions.role: highest-varna group whose honor is protected by asymmetric fine schedules

mentions.quote: For a Brahmana, it shall be sixty-fourfold, or a full hundred, or even twice sixty-four; for he is a knower of the good and bad qualities of that act
mentions.role: subject of graduated theft-fine schedule, bearing the heaviest moral responsibility

mentions.quote: No greater non-Dharma is known on earth than the slaying of a Brahmana
mentions.role: protected group whose killing is declared the supreme transgression

mentions.quote: in the defense of women and Brahmanas, one who slays according to Dharma is not tainted
mentions.role: group whose defense legitimates defensive killing

entities.description: The priestly varna occupying the highest rank in the social hierarchy, subject to the strictest moral expectations, the most severe moral fines, and the strongest protections against violence.
entities.justification: Brahmanas appear in dozens of verses throughout the window as the normative reference point for fines, punishments, and social protections, confirming their centrality to the window's legal framework.

mentions.quote: A Kshatriya who insults a Brahmana deserves a fine of one hundred
mentions.role: second-varna group subject to asymmetric verbal-assault fines

mentions.quote: of a Kshatriya, thirty-twofold
mentions.role: second-varna group in the graduated theft-fine schedule

mentions.quote: a Kshatriya shall be fined a thousand and deserves to have his head shaved with urine
mentions.role: second-varna group subject to sexual-offense punishments

entities.description: The warrior-ruler varna ranked second in the social hierarchy, subject to intermediate fines for verbal, physical, and sexual offenses across the legal code.
entities.justification: Kshatriyas recur throughout the fine and punishment schedules as the second benchmark varna, establishing their consistent position in the text's normative framework.

mentions.quote: a Vaishya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred
mentions.role: third-varna group in verbal-assault fine schedule

mentions.quote: of a Vaishya, sixteenfold
mentions.role: third-varna group in graduated theft-fine schedule

mentions.quote: He should make a Vaishya engage in trade, money-lending, and agriculture, and also in the protection of cattle
mentions.role: group whose prescribed social duties are enumerated by the lawgiver

entities.description: The merchant-farmer varna ranked third in the social hierarchy, whose prescribed occupations are trade, agriculture, and cattle-herding, and who face intermediate fines.
entities.justification: Vaishyas appear throughout the window in fine schedules and in the prescription of varna-specific duties, establishing their consistent middle-varna position.

mentions.quote: A man of a single birth who assails the twice-born with harsh speech shall have his tongue cut out, for he is of low origin
mentions.role: low-born group subject to corporal punishment for verbal transgression

mentions.quote: the guilt of a Shudra shall be eightfold
mentions.role: lowest varna in the graduated theft-fine schedule

mentions.quote: he should make a Shudra perform the work of a slave, whether bought or not bought; for he was created by the Self-existent One for the service of a Brahmana
mentions.role: group whose servitude is cosmologically grounded and legally enforced

mentions.quote: A Shudra, even if released by his master, is not freed from servitude; for that is innate in him
mentions.role: group defined by inalienable hereditary servitude

entities.description: The lowest varna in the social hierarchy, subject to corporal punishments for verbal offenses and prescribed by the text as constitutionally bound to servile labor.
entities.justification: Shudras appear throughout the window at the base of every fine and punishment scale and are the explicit subject of extended discussion of hereditary servitude at the window's close.

mentions.quote: for intercourse with a Vratya woman, and likewise with a Chandala woman, it is the same
mentions.role: outcast group whose women are marked as objects of aggravated sexual offense

entities.description: An outcast group placed below the four varnas whose women are referenced in the sexual offense schedule alongside Vratya women.
entities.justification: The Chandala woman is named as a distinct category in the punishment schedule for sexual offenses, marking the group's position outside and below the varna hierarchy.

mentions.quote: for intercourse with a Vratya woman, and likewise with a Chandala woman, it is the same
mentions.role: ritually degraded group referenced in the sexual offense fine schedule

entities.description: A ritually irregular or degraded group whose women are listed alongside Chandala women as a category attracting doubled fines for sexual offenses after a year's accusation.
entities.justification: Vratya women are named as a distinct penalty category in Mn_8.373, grounding the entry in the text.

mentions.quote: The Adhvaryu should take the chariot, and the Brahma priest the horse at the establishment of the fire
mentions.role: ritual officiant assigned specific sacrificial fees

entities.description: The Adhvaryu is the Vedic priest responsible for the ritual actions in a sacrifice, assigned the chariot as his fee at the establishment of the fire.
entities.justification: The Adhvaryu is named with a specific fee-assignment at Mn_8.209, grounding him as a distinct ritual functionary in the sacrificial fee dispute section.

mentions.quote: the Hotri priest may also take a horse
mentions.role: ritual officiant assigned a horse as his share of sacrificial fees

entities.description: The Vedic reciter-priest (Hotri) who chants hymns at sacrifices and is assigned a horse as part of the fee distribution at the fire-establishment ceremony.
entities.justification: The Hotri priest is named at Mn_8.209 in the context of fee allocation, confirming his presence in the text.

mentions.quote: the Udgatri priest a cart at the purchase of Soma
mentions.role: ritual officiant assigned a cart as his share of sacrificial fees

entities.description: The Vedic chanter-priest (Udgatri) who sings the Samaveda hymns and is assigned a cart as his fee at the Soma-purchasing rite.
entities.justification: The Udgatri priest is named at Mn_8.209 with a distinct fee-assignment, confirming his presence in this ritual-fee dispute passage.

mentions.quote: the Brahma priest the horse at the establishment of the fire
mentions.role: overseer-priest assigned a horse as his share of sacrificial fees

entities.description: The Brahma (overseer) priest at Vedic sacrifices who supervises the entire rite and is assigned a horse as fee at the fire-establishment ceremony.
entities.justification: The Brahma priest is named at Mn_8.209 alongside the other three main officiants, grounding the entry in the text.

mentions.quote: a wolf should attack while the herdsman is not present, for any that the wolf seizes and kills, the guilt shall be the herdsman's
mentions.role: natural predator whose attack on penned livestock triggers herdsman liability

mentions.quote: a wolf should leap up and kill one, the herdsman is not guilty in that case
mentions.role: natural predator whose attack on grazing livestock does not trigger herdsman liability

entities.description: A wild predatory animal used in the text to distinguish two scenarios of livestock loss — one triggering and one exempting herdsman liability.
entities.justification: The wolf appears in two consecutive verses (Mn_8.235-236) as the operative agent in distinct liability determinations, making it a legally significant animal entity.

themes.topic: Varna hierarchy and differential legal treatment

mentions.quote: A Kshatriya who insults a Brahmana deserves a fine of one hundred; a Vaishya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Shudra deserves corporal punishment
For a theft, the guilt of a Shudra shall be eightfold; of a Vaishya, sixteenfold; of a Kshatriya, thirty-twofold
For a Brahmana, it shall be sixty-fourfold, or a full hundred, or even twice sixty-four

themes.justification: The entire window from Mn_8.267 onward organizes verbal assault, physical assault, theft, and sexual offense punishments along varna lines, making differential treatment by social rank the dominant structural principle of the legal code.

themes.topic: Royal duty to protect subjects and punish wrongdoers

mentions.quote: A sixth part of the Dharma from all belongs to the king who protects; but a sixth part of the non-Dharma also belongs to him who does not protect
A king should make the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves; for by the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase
That king who, without protecting, takes tribute, taxes, tolls, and a share of fines, he goes immediately to hell

themes.justification: Multiple verses (Mn_8.302-311) elaborate that the king's legitimacy derives entirely from protection: collecting revenue without protection is tantamount to theft, and the king earns or forfeits a portion of the moral merit/demerit of his subjects depending on whether he protects them.

themes.topic: Property, debt, and deposits — contractual obligations

mentions.quote: A wise man should make a deposit with one who is of noble family, of good conduct, who knows the Dharma
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands what he has not deposited, both should be punished like a thief
Where enjoyment is seen, but no title is seen anywhere, there the title is the cause, not the enjoyment

themes.justification: A substantial portion of the window (Mn_8.179-202) deals systematically with deposits, sealed deposits, fraudulent sales, and title-vs-possession disputes, establishing a law of contract and bailment.

themes.topic: Theft — classification, graduated punishment, and limits

mentions.quote: For one who steals more than ten kumbhas of grain, the punishment is death; for less, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value
With whatever limb a thief acts among men, that very limb the king should take away from him, for the sake of setting an example
Fruit and roots from a wild tree, wood for the sake of a fire, and likewise grass for the sake of feeding cows — Manu has declared this not to be theft

themes.justification: Mn_8.302-343 devotes an extended passage to theft: categories of stolen goods, quantity thresholds for death vs. mutilation vs. fines, varna-multiplied guilt, exceptions for travelers and forest produce, and the ritual of self-surrender to the king.

themes.topic: Sexual offenses and the protection of women

mentions.quote: For from that arises the mixing of varnas in the world, by which root-destroying non-Dharma is produced, leading to the destruction of all
He who defiles an unwilling maiden shall immediately receive the punishment of death
A non-Brahmana deserves the punishment of death for adultery; for the wives of all four varnas must always be most carefully protected

themes.justification: Mn_8.352-385 systematically catalogs offenses against women — adultery, rape, consensual intercourse across varna lines — and derives punishments from the varna combination of perpetrator and victim, with varna mixing as the ultimate social danger.

mentions.quote: When a dispute has arisen between two villages concerning a boundary, he should settle the boundary in the month of Jyeshtha, when the boundary marks are most visible
He should make boundary-trees, such as banyans, pipal trees, and palashas, silk-cotton trees, sal and palm trees, and also milky trees
By these marks, the king should settle the boundary between two disputing parties

themes.justification: Mn_8.245-265 constitutes an extended treatment of boundary law: seasonal timing of surveys, material markers (trees, buried objects, landmarks), witness procedures, and penalties for false testimony — covering the full procedural and evidentiary framework for land disputes.

themes.topic: Legitimate use of force and self-defense

mentions.quote: A weapon may be taken up by the twice-born when Dharma is obstructed, and in a calamity caused by time that afflicts the twice-born and the varnas
in the protection of oneself, and in a conflict over sacrificial fees, and in the defense of women and Brahmanas, one who slays according to Dharma is not tainted
There is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in the slaying of an aggressor, whether openly or secretly; fury meets fury

themes.justification: Mn_8.348-351 constitutes an explicit statement of justified homicide, carving out contexts in which killing is dharmically permissible — defense of self, women, Brahmanas, and sacrificial property — making legitimate force a distinct doctrinal theme.

themes.topic: Hereditary servitude and the Shudra's ontological status

mentions.quote: he should make a Shudra perform the work of a slave, whether bought or not bought; for he was created by the Self-existent One for the service of a Brahmana
A Shudra, even if released by his master, is not freed from servitude; for that is innate in him

One captured under a banner, one who becomes a slave for food, one born in the house, one who is bought, one who is given, one inherited from his father, and one who becomes a slave to pay off a fine — these are the seven origins of slaves

themes.justification: The window closes with Mn_8.413-415 making the boldest ontological claim in the chapter: Shudra servitude is innate, divinely ordained, and inalienable, culminating in a taxonomy of seven categories of slaves — giving hereditary servitude its own concluding doctrinal section.

themes.topic: Karma, merit transfer, and eschatological consequences of kingship

mentions.quote: The slayer of a learned Brahmana wipes his sin on one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife, on her husband; a pupil and one for whom a sacrifice is performed, on the guru; and a thief, on the king
a thief, on the king
men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings, they go to heaven, pure, like the virtuous who have done good deeds
the king becomes a sharer of the sixth part by means of righteous protection

themes.justification: An implicit theological framework pervades the section: punishment purifies the offender, transferring sin to the negligent king; righteous protection earns the king a fraction of every subject's religious merit — establishing a karmic economy of royal governance not stated as a separate doctrine but underlying multiple verses.

themes.topic: Regulation of commerce, wages, and market conduct

mentions.quote: those who are skilled and expert in all merchandise should fix the price according to the goods, and from that the king should take a twentieth part
One who avoids a toll-station, who buys or sells at an improper time, and one who speaks falsely in counting shall be made to pay a fine of eight times the amount
The balance, the weights, and the measures should all be well-marked; and every six months, he should examine them again

themes.justification: Mn_8.396-409 covers weaver fees, toll-station duties, price-fixing procedures, standardization of weights and measures, and ferry-tolls — constituting a coherent section on market regulation and royal economic governance.
